Photography on a Motorcycle Tour

Half the joy of a motorcycle tour is sharing it afterwards — and great photos make the stories come alive. You don't need expensive gear or professional skills. With a few simple techniques, your touring photos will go from snapshots to something worth framing.

Camera Options for Touring

  • Smartphone: Modern phones take excellent photos and are always with you. The best camera is the one you actually use. Protect it in a waterproof case.
  • Action camera (GoPro etc): Great for helmet-mounted video and POV shots. Waterproof, rugged, and captures the riding experience uniquely.
  • Compact camera: Something like a Sony RX100 or Ricoh GR gives you much better image quality than a phone in a small package.
  • Mirrorless/DSLR: Best image quality but adds weight and bulk. Only worth it if photography is a major part of your tour. Pack in a padded, waterproof bag.

Composition Tips for Touring Photos

These simple rules transform average photos into great ones:

  • Rule of thirds: Place your motorcycle or the horizon on a third line, not dead centre. Most phones have a grid overlay to help.
  • Include the road: A winding road disappearing into the distance is the classic touring shot. Stand back and let the road draw the eye through the frame.
  • Use your bike as foreground: Park your motorcycle with a stunning backdrop and use it as an anchor point. The bike gives scale and context to landscapes.
  • Get low: Crouch down for a low angle. This makes the bike look more dramatic and the sky more imposing.
  • Frame within frames: Use arches, doorways, tree branches, or bridge structures to frame your subject.

Best Times to Photograph

  • Golden hour: The first and last hour of sunlight produces warm, soft light. Plan to be at a viewpoint during golden hour for the best landscape shots.
  • Blue hour: The 30 minutes before sunrise and after sunset give a beautiful blue tone. Great for moody highland shots.
  • Overcast days: Don't dismiss cloud cover — it provides even, soft light that's perfect for detail shots, forest roads, and castle ruins.
  • Rainy aftermath: Wet roads, shiny surfaces, and breaking clouds after rain produce some of the most dramatic images.
The best touring photos tell a story. Don't just photograph the view — include your bike, your gear, the coffee stop, the winding road. These details capture the feeling of the tour, not just the places.

Practical Tips for Rider Photographers

  • Plan your stops: Identify viewpoints and photo spots on your route in advance. Rushing past because you didn't know the viewpoint was there means missed shots.
  • Carry a mini tripod: A Gorillapod weighs nothing and lets you take sharp long-exposure shots or include yourself in the frame using a timer.
  • Protect your gear: Use a waterproof dry bag inside your luggage. Even waterproof panniers can let moisture in over a long wet day.
  • Back up daily: Transfer photos to a cloud service (Google Photos, iCloud) at the end of each day when you have WiFi. Losing a week's photos to a dropped phone or camera is devastating.
  • Clean your lens: Road grime, rain, and finger marks accumulate fast. Carry a microfibre cloth and use it often.

Action Shots of Your Ride

  • Use an action camera on a chin mount for the rider's-eye view — the most engaging perspective for video.
  • For photos of your bike in motion, you need a riding partner. Ask them to pull ahead and photograph you approaching, or set up at a corner with a burst mode.
  • Slow shutter speeds (1/30th second) from a mounted camera create motion blur that conveys speed. This requires a stable mount.

Touring photography isn't about perfection — it's about memory. Take hundreds of photos, be creative, and don't spend so long behind the lens that you forget to enjoy the view with your own eyes. Read our Best Touring Helmets for UK Motorcycle Adventures 2026 guide for more.
keyTakeaways: The best camera is the one you actually use; modern smartphones handle most touring shots well.
Use the rule of thirds and include a winding road or your bike as a foreground anchor for scale.
Golden hour and blue hour give the warmest and moodiest light; overcast days suit detail and forest shots.
Carry a Gorillapod mini tripod and back up photos to the cloud each evening on WiFi.
Action cameras on a chin mount capture the most engaging rider's-eye video.

faq.q: When is the best time of day to photograph a tour?
faq.a: Golden hour, the first and last hour of sunlight, produces warm, soft light ideal for landscapes, so plan to be at a viewpoint then. Blue hour, the 30 minutes before sunrise and after sunset, gives a beautiful moody tone for Highland scenes. Do not dismiss overcast days either, as flat cloud light suits detail shots, forest roads and castle ruins.

faq.q: How do I get an action shot of myself riding?
faq.a: For moving shots of your own bike you need a riding partner: ask them to pull ahead and photograph you approaching, or set up at a corner using burst mode. A chin-mounted action camera captures the rider's-eye view for video. Slow shutter speeds around 1/30th second from a stable mount add motion blur that conveys speed.

faq.q: How do I protect camera gear from UK weather?
faq.a: Keep everything electronic in a waterproof dry bag inside your luggage, because even waterproof panniers can let moisture in over a long wet day. Carry a microfibre cloth to wipe road grime, rain and finger marks off the lens frequently, and back up your photos to a cloud service each evening so a dropped phone does not cost you the whole trip.

faq.q: Do I need an expensive camera for good touring photos?
faq.a: No. A modern smartphone with the grid overlay switched on for the rule of thirds will produce excellent results. Composition, timing and light matter far more than the gear. Include the road and your bike for scale, get low for drama, and take plenty of shots. Spend your budget on a small tripod before a bigger camera.
